module.title: 3 · Two-Stage Least Squares
module.summary: Project x on the instruments, then regress y on the fitted x to recover a consistent β₁.

stages.title: The two stages
stages.html:
2SLS in two moves

Two-Stage Least Squares operationalises the instrument idea:

  • First stage. Regress the endogenous x on the instrument(s) z (and any exogenous controls):
    x = π₀ + π₁·z + v. Keep the fitted values x̂. These are the part of x predicted by z — the clean, exogenous slice.
  • Second stage. Regress y on x̂ instead of x:
    y = β₀ + β₁·x̂ + error. Because x̂ is built only from z, it is uncorrelated with the confounder, so β̂₁ is consistent.
Key idea. x̂ strips out the contaminated variation in x and keeps only the variation z explains. Regressing on x̂ is like running the experiment z would have run for you.

With one endogenous regressor and one instrument the model is just-identified and 2SLS equals the simple IV ratio Cov(z,y)/Cov(z,x). With more instruments than endogenous regressors it is over-identified (Module 4).

stages.title: Do it in one call — and mind the SEs
stages.html:
Use a built-in estimator

You can run the two regressions by hand, but doing the second stage manually with sm.OLS(y, x̂) produces wrong standard errors: it ignores that x̂ is estimated, not observed. Use a dedicated estimator that corrects for this:

IV2SLS(endog, exog, instrument).fit()

The statsmodels signature (from statsmodels.sandbox.regression.gmm) is:

  • endog = y
  • exog = the regressors in the structural equation — the constant and the endogenous x (plus any exogenous controls)
  • instrument = the constant and the instrument z (plus the same exogenous controls, which instrument themselves)

Build both design matrices with sm.add_constant. The point estimate matches the manual two-stage fit, but the reported SEs are now correct.

Key idea. Manual two-stage = right coefficient, wrong SE. IV2SLS = right coefficient and right SE.

stages.title: OLS bias vs consistent 2SLS
stages.note: Same data, three estimators. OLS is pulled up by the confounder; the hand-built two-stage and IV2SLS both land near the true β₁ = 2. Note the manual second stage prints a WRONG SE.
stages.code:
import numpy as np, statsmodels.api as sm, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from statsmodels.sandbox.regression.gmm import IV2SLS
rng = np.random.default_rng(0); n=1000
u = rng.normal(0,1,n)                 # confounder
z = rng.normal(0,1,n)                 # instrument
x = 1.2*z + 1.0*u + rng.normal(0,1,n) # endogenous (shares u with y)
y = 1 + 2*x + 3*u + rng.normal(0,1,n) # true beta1 = 2

# OLS (biased)
ols = sm.OLS(y, sm.add_constant(x)).fit()
# Manual two-stage: project x on z, then regress y on x-hat
xhat = sm.OLS(x, sm.add_constant(z)).fit().fittedvalues
man  = sm.OLS(y, sm.add_constant(xhat)).fit()
# Proper IV2SLS (correct SEs)
exog = sm.add_constant(x); instr = sm.add_constant(z)
iv   = IV2SLS(y, exog, instr).fit()

print(f'true beta1            = 2.000')
print(f'OLS    beta1_hat      = {ols.params[1]:.3f}   SE {ols.bse[1]:.3f}  (biased up)')
print(f'manual 2-stage beta1  = {man.params[1]:.3f}   (SE here is WRONG: {man.bse[1]:.3f})')
print(f'IV2SLS beta1_hat      = {iv.params[1]:.3f}   SE {iv.bse[1]:.3f}  (consistent, correct SE)')

plt.figure(figsize=(6,3.7))
labels=['OLS','IV2SLS']; vals=[ols.params[1],iv.params[1]]; errs=[ols.bse[1],iv.bse[1]]
plt.bar(labels,vals,yerr=errs,capsize=6,color=['#c9c6ac','#da9100'])
plt.axhline(2,color='#af983f',ls='--',lw=2,label='true = 2'); plt.legend()
plt.title(f'OLS {ols.params[1]:.2f}  vs  2SLS {iv.params[1]:.2f}')

stages.title: Confounding slider: OLS drifts, 2SLS holds
stages.note: Increase γ (effect of the confounder on y). OLS marches away from 2; as long as the instrument stays valid, 2SLS stays anchored near the truth.
stages.template:
import numpy as np, statsmodels.api as sm
from statsmodels.sandbox.regression.gmm import IV2SLS
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
rng=np.random.default_rng(0); n=1000
u=rng.normal(0,1,n); z=rng.normal(0,1,n)
x=1.2*z+1.0*u+rng.normal(0,1,n)
y=1+2*x+{{gamma}}*u+rng.normal(0,1,n)
ols=sm.OLS(y,sm.add_constant(x)).fit().params[1]
iv =IV2SLS(y,sm.add_constant(x),sm.add_constant(z)).fit().params[1]
plt.figure(figsize=(6,3.7))
plt.bar(['OLS','2SLS'],[ols,iv],color=['#c9c6ac','#da9100'])
plt.axhline(2,color='#af983f',ls='--',lw=2,label='true=2'); plt.legend()
plt.title(f'gamma={{gamma}}:  OLS={ols:.2f}   2SLS={iv:.2f}')

stages.title: Check: what goes into the second stage?
stages.prompt: In 2SLS, the second-stage regression of y is run on…
choices: the fitted values x̂ from regressing x on the instruments
the residuals from the first stage
stages.hint: We want the clean part of x that z explains.
stages.explain: The second stage uses x̂, the projection of x onto the instruments. Because x̂ is built only from exogenous z, it is uncorrelated with the confounder, giving a consistent β̂₁.

stages.title: Check: why not hand-roll the SEs?
stages.prompt: Why prefer IV2SLS over manually running sm.OLS(y, x̂) for the second stage?
choices: The manual standard errors are wrong because they ignore that x̂ is estimated
IV2SLS uses a different, larger sample
There is no difference at all
stages.hint: The point estimate matches; something else does not.
stages.explain: Both give the same β̂₁, but plugging x̂ into a naive OLS understates uncertainty because it treats the generated regressor as if it were observed. IV2SLS corrects the variance.

stages.title: The clean slice of x
stages.lead: 2SLS runs in two moves: regress x on the instruments, keep the predictions, then run the structural equation on those.
stages.prompt: In 2SLS the second stage regresses y not on the raw endogenous x, but on the ___ values x̂ that the first stage predicts from the instruments.
stages.hint: It's the part of x that z explains — the clean, exogenous slice, written x̂.
stages.explain: The blank is fitted (predicted) values, x̂. The misconception this defuses is 'plug the instrument z straight into the second stage' — you regress y on x̂, not on z and not on the first-stage residuals. x̂ keeps only the variation in x that z explains, stripping out the confounded part. Boundary: with one instrument and one endogenous regressor this two-stage fit numerically equals the simple IV ratio Cov(z,y)/Cov(z,x); with extra instruments it does not, which is the over-identified case.

stages.title: Hand-rolled second-stage SEs
stages.prompt: Claim: running the second stage by hand with sm.OLS(y, x̂) gives both the right 2SLS coefficient and the right standard errors.
stages.hint: The point estimate matches; think about what x̂ being estimated (not observed) does to the uncertainty.
stages.explain: This is the manual-2SLS-is-fine trap. The hand-rolled coefficient is correct, but the standard errors are wrong: sm.OLS(y, x̂) treats x̂ as if it were observed data, ignoring that x̂ was itself estimated in the first stage, so it understates the true sampling variability. Use a dedicated IV2SLS estimator, which corrects the SEs. Boundary: the bias is only in the inference (SEs, t-stats, CIs) — the β̂ from the manual route is identical, so the fix is the SE formula, not the point estimate.
